title: A treatment can do better in every group and still look worse overall
body: Simpson’s paradox happens when a trend that shows up in several groups of data disappears or reverses once the groups are combined. It isn’t an arithmetic mistake: it arises when the groups differ in size and in some hidden factor, a confounder, that also affects the outcome. The lesson is that pooled totals can mislead, and you have to ask what is driving the numbers before concluding anything about cause and effect.

slides.heading: A real example
slides.text: A 1986 study compared two kidney stone treatments. Treatment A had the higher success rate for small stones (93% vs 87%) and for large stones (73% vs 69%).

slides.heading: The reversal
slides.text: Yet with all patients pooled, treatment B looked better: about 83% success versus 78% for A. How can A win both rounds and still lose overall?

slides.heading: The hidden factor
slides.text: Treatment A was mostly used on large stones, the harder cases that fail more often, while B mostly got easy small stones. Stone size skewed the totals.

slides.question: In the kidney stone study, why did treatment A look worse overall?
options: The percentages were added up wrongly
B’s patients were younger and fitter
A was mostly used on the harder cases
A’s small-stone results were left out
slides.explanation: Treatment A was mostly given for large stones, the harder cases that fail more often, while B mostly got easy small stones. Stone size, the hidden factor, skewed the totals.
